title: Shortcuts: comprehensions
summary: Build lists, sets and dictionaries from other collections in one readable line.

sources.section: 6.2.4. Displays for lists, sets and dictionaries

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Build lists and dictionaries in one expression with comprehensions, filtering as you go.
analogy: A comprehension is a sieve with a stamp: items fall through the filter, get stamped by the expression, and land in a new container.

misconceptions.belief: A comprehension changes the original list.
misconceptions.correction: It builds a new list or dict; the source is left alone.

misconceptions.belief: The `if` goes before the `for` to filter.
misconceptions.correction: A filter goes after: `[x for x in xs if x > 0]`; `a if c else b` before `for` chooses a value instead.

misconceptions.belief: A dict comprehension can keep two values for the same key.
misconceptions.correction: A later item with the same key replaces the earlier one.

rubric.evidence: the result is built by a comprehension, not a loop with append
exactly the wanted items are kept
lists where order matters, dicts for lookups by key

review.recall: Write from memory a list comprehension that keeps the even numbers from xs and squares them.

steps.title: The same three lines, again and again
steps.body:
You've written this pattern many times: start an empty list, loop, maybe test, append. It works, but
the *point* of the code ("the squares of the even numbers") is spread over three or four lines.
A **comprehension** says the same thing in one line that reads almost like the sentence.

steps.title: Describe the result, not the steps
steps.body:
Read `[n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]` from the inside out: *for each `n` in `numbers`, if it
is even, put `n * n` in the new list.* It is exactly the build-a-list loop, folded into one
expression that **produces a new list** and leaves `numbers` untouched.

The same shape with braces builds a dictionary (`{key: value for ...}`) or a set (`{x for ...}`).

questions: Rewrite `[w.upper() for w in words]` as a loop in your head. What does each part become?
When would a normal loop be clearer than a comprehension?

steps.title: A comprehension unrolled
steps.body: This loop does exactly what `[n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]` does. Watch the result grow.

frames.note: The comprehension's brackets: a new, empty list.
The `if` part: 1 is odd, so nothing is added.
2 passes the test; the expression part `n * n` adds 4.
The finished new list. `nums` was never changed.
Same result as the one-line comprehension.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
```python
[expression for name in iterable]              # a new list
[expression for name in iterable if condition] # only items passing the test
{key: value for name in iterable}              # a new dictionary
{expression for name in iterable}              # a new set (no duplicates)
```

1. The result is always a **new** collection. Building it doesn't change the iterable, though an
   expression or condition that calls a mutating method (e.g. `x.append(...)`) still can, so keep them pure.
2. Items are visited in order; `expression` is evaluated once for each item that passes `condition`.
3. In a dict comprehension, a repeated key keeps the **last** value produced for it.
4. The loop name (`name`) belongs to the comprehension and does not leak out into your code.
5. Keep them short. If you need several steps, `print`s or `try`, write an ordinary loop.

steps.title: Run it: three comprehensions
steps.body: Predict each line, including what the set comprehension does with the duplicate.
steps.code:
words = ["apple", "Bob", "cat", "apple"]
print([w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 3])
print({w: len(w) for w in words})
print(sorted({w[0].lower() for w in words}))

steps.title: Your turn: tidy the readings
steps.body:
Complete `positive_rounded(readings)` with a **single list comprehension** (a check looks for exactly one
comprehension loop and no `.append`) that keeps only readings
above 0 and rounds each to a whole number with `round(r)`. The input list must not change.
steps.starter:
def positive_rounded(readings):
    return [r for r in readings]
hints: Add an `if` part to filter: only readings where `r > 0`.
Change the expression part from `r` to `round(r)`.

def positive_rounded(readings):
    return [round(r) for r in readings if r > 0]

tests.name: empty
tests.code: assert positive_rounded([]) == [], 'an empty list gives an empty list'

tests.name: input unchanged
tests.code:
_data = [2.2, -1.0]
positive_rounded(_data)
assert _data == [2.2, -1.0], 'do not change the input'

tests.name: uses one list comprehension
tests.code:
import dis
_ops, _names, _todo = [], set(), [positive_rounded.__code__]
while _todo:
    _c = _todo.pop()
    _ops += [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(_c)]
    _names |= set(_c.co_names)
    _todo += [k for k in _c.co_consts if hasattr(k, 'co_code')]
assert 'LIST_APPEND' in _ops and 'append' not in _names and _ops.count('FOR_ITER') == 1, 'write it as one list comprehension, [... for r in readings if ...], not a loop with append'

steps.solution:
def positive_rounded(readings):
    return [round(r) for r in readings if r > 0]

steps.title: Challenge: an index of word lengths
steps.body:
Write `length_index(words)` returning a dictionary that maps each **lower-case** word to its length,
but only for words of at least 3 letters: `length_index(["Hi", "Owl", "swan"])` is
`{"owl": 3, "swan": 4}`. Use a dictionary comprehension (a check looks for one).
steps.starter:
def length_index(words):
    return {w: len(w) for w in words}
hints: Two things are missing: lower-casing the key, and the length filter.
The key expression can be `w.lower()`; the filter is `if len(w) >= 3`.

def length_index(words):
    return {w.lower(): len(w) for w in words if len(w) >= 3}

tests.name: nothing qualifies
tests.code: assert length_index(['a', 'to']) == {}, 'no word has 3 or more letters'

tests.name: uses a dict comprehension
tests.code:
import dis
_ops, _names, _todo = [], set(), [length_index.__code__]
while _todo:
    _c = _todo.pop()
    _ops += [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(_c)]
    _names |= set(_c.co_names)
    _todo += [k for k in _c.co_consts if hasattr(k, 'co_code')]
assert 'MAP_ADD' in _ops and _ops.count('FOR_ITER') == 1, 'build the result with one dictionary comprehension, {key: value for w in words if ...}'

steps.solution:
def length_index(words):
    return {w.lower(): len(w) for w in words if len(w) >= 3}

steps.title: Transfer: a price list
steps.body:
Write `square_evens(numbers)`, which returns the squares of the even numbers, in order, using a list comprehension.
Then write `price_index(items)`, where `items` is a list of `(name, price)` pairs: return a dict from each name in
lower case to its price, keeping only items with a price above 0.
hints: `[n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]`.
`{name.lower(): price for name, price in items if price > 0}`.

tests.name: squares of the evens, in order
names in lower case, priced items only
a later price replaces an earlier one
square_evens uses a list comprehension
tests.code:
import ast
_fn = next(n for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(__source__)) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == 'square_evens')
assert any(isinstance(n, ast.ListComp) for n in ast.walk(_fn)), 'build the list with a list comprehension'

questions.explanation: Only items passing the `if` test are kept; the expression is just `x`.
A repeated key keeps the last value produced for it.

questions.prompt: After `nums = [1, 2]` and `[n * 10 for n in nums]`, what is `nums`?
questions.explanation: A comprehension builds a new list; the original is unchanged (and the result here was not stored).

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Turn a build-a-list loop into `[expression for name in iterable if condition]`.
- Build dictionaries and sets the same way, knowing repeated keys keep the last value.
- Choose a plain loop when the logic needs more than one simple step.
